1.5 Rules for derivatives

Some useful rules for derivatives to apply are:

Rulef(x)f(x)f(x)f′(x)f'(x)f′(x)
Constantkkk0
Powerxnx^nxn, n≠0n \ne 0n=0nxn−1nx^{n-1}nxn−1
Multipleku(x)k u(x)ku(x)ku′(x)k u'(x)ku′(x)
Sumu(x)+v(x)u(x) + v(x)u(x)+v(x)u′(x)+v′(x)u'(x) + v'(x)u′(x)+v′(x)
Differenceu(x)−v(x)u(x) - v(x)u(x)−v(x)u′(x)−v′(x)u'(x) - v'(x)u′(x)−v′(x)
Exponentialaxa^xaxaxln⁡aa^x \ln aaxlna
Logarithmlog⁡ax\log_a xloga​x1xln⁡a\dfrac{1}{x \ln a}xlna1​

Note that two special cases of the last two derivatives occur when a=ea = ea=e:

d⁡ ⁣exd⁡ ⁣x=exd⁡ ⁣ln⁡xd⁡ ⁣x=1x\dd{}{e^x}{x} = e^x \qquad \dd{}{\ln x}{x} = \frac{1}{x}dxdex​=exdxdlnx​=x1​
(1)

Here are some examples showing how to explicitly apply them:

f(x)=x3\displaystyle f(x) = x^3f(x)=x3

f′(x)=3x3−1=3x2f'(x) = 3x^{3-1} = 3x^2f′(x)=3x3−1=3x2
(2)

f(x)=−x2+3\displaystyle f(x) = -x^2 + 3f(x)=−x2+3

f′(x)=ddx(−x2)+ddx(3)=−ddx(x2)+ddx(3)=−2x2−1+0=−2x\begin{align} f'(x) &= \frac{d}{dx}(-x^2) + \frac{d}{dx}(3) \\ &= -\frac{d}{dx}(x^2) + \frac{d}{dx}(3) \\ &= -2x^{2-1} + 0 \\ &= -2x \end{align}f′(x)​=dxd​(−x2)+dxd​(3)=−dxd​(x2)+dxd​(3)=−2x2−1+0=−2x​​
(3)

f(x)=4x33−x+2ex\displaystyle f(x) = \frac{4x^3}{3} - x + 2e^xf(x)=34x3​−x+2ex

f′(x)=43ddx(x3)−ddx(x)+2ddx(ex)=43(3x2)−1+2ex=4x2−1+2ex\begin{align} f'(x) &= \frac{4}{3} \frac{d}{dx}(x^3) - \frac{d}{dx}(x) + 2 \frac{d}{dx}(e^x) \\ &= \frac{4}{3}(3x^2) - 1 + 2e^x \\ &= 4x^2 - 1 + 2e^x \end{align}f′(x)​=34​dxd​(x3)−dxd​(x)+2dxd​(ex)=34​(3x2)−1+2ex=4x2−1+2ex​​
(4)

f(x)=3x2+x\displaystyle f(x) = \frac{3}{x^2} + \sqrt{x}f(x)=x23​+x​

f′(x)=3ddx(x−2)+ddx(x1/2)=3(−2x−3)+12x−1/2=−6x3+12x\begin{align} f'(x) &= 3 \frac{d}{dx}(x^{-2}) + \frac{d}{dx}(x^{1/2}) \\ &= 3(-2x^{-3}) + \frac{1}{2} x^{-1/2} \\ &= \frac{-6}{x^3} + \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}} \end{align}f′(x)​=3dxd​(x−2)+dxd​(x1/2)=3(−2x−3)+21​x−1/2=x3−6​+2x​1​​​
(5)

f(x)=log⁡(4x)f(x) = \log(4x)f(x)=log(4x)

f′(x)=ddx[log⁡4+log⁡x]=ddx(log⁡4)+ddx(log⁡x)=0+1xln⁡10\begin{align} f'(x) &= \frac{d}{dx} [\log 4 + \log x] \\ &= \frac{d}{dx}(\log 4) + \frac{d}{dx}(\log x) \\ &= 0 + \frac{1}{x \ln 10} \end{align}f′(x)​=dxd​[log4+logx]=dxd​(log4)+dxd​(logx)=0+xln101​​​
(6)

There are other rules related to functions that are products, quotients, compositions, or trigonometric. We will go over each of those in more detail next.

Product rule¶

The product rule is used to differentiate functions that can be written as the product of two smaller functions.

Product rule

If f(x)=u(x)v(x)f(x) = u(x) v(x)f(x)=u(x)v(x), then

f′=uv′+vu′=ud⁡ ⁣vd⁡ ⁣x+vd⁡ ⁣ud⁡ ⁣x\begin{align} f' &= u v' + v u ' \\ &= u \dd{}{v}{x} + v \dd{}{u}{x} \end{align}f′​=uv′+vu′=udxdv​+vdxdu​​​
(7)

To demonstrate this rule, consider f(x)=(x−3)(x−1)f(x) = (x-3)(x-1)f(x)=(x−3)(x−1). Previously, we would have needed to expand this function before differentiating:

f(x)=x2−4x+3f′(x)=2x−4\begin{align} f(x) &= x^2 - 4x + 3 \\ f'(x) &= 2x - 4 \end{align}f(x)f′(x)​=x2−4x+3=2x−4​​
(8)

With the product rule, instead we recognize

u=x−3v=x−1u′=1v′=1\begin{align} u &= x-3 & v &= x-1 \\ u' &= 1 & v' &= 1 \end{align}uu′​=x−3=1​vv′​=x−1=1​​
(9)

so

f′(x)=uv′+vu′=(x−3)⋅1+(x−1)⋅1=2x−4f'(x) = uv' + vu' = (x-3) \cdot 1 + (x-1) \cdot 1 = 2x - 4f′(x)=uv′+vu′=(x−3)⋅1+(x−1)⋅1=2x−4
(10)

This example is a little silly, but the product rule is a life saver for functions that are hard to expand! Here are some better examples:

f(x)=(x+1)(2x2+5)(5x3−4)f(x) = (x+1)(2x^2 + 5)(5x^3-4)f(x)=(x+1)(2x2+5)(5x3−4)

Identify:

u=x+1v=(2x2+5)(5x3−4)u = x+1 \qquad v = (2x^2+5)(5x^3-4)u=x+1v=(2x2+5)(5x3−4)
(11)

so

f′(x)=(x+1)v′+(2x2+5)(5x3−4)(1)f'(x) = (x+1)v' + (2x^2 +5)(5x^3-4)(1)f′(x)=(x+1)v′+(2x2+5)(5x3−4)(1)
(12)

The derivative v′v'v′ can be evaluated by a second product rule!

u=2x2+5v=5x3−4u′=4xv′=15x2\begin{align} u &= 2x^2+5 & v &= 5x^3-4 \\ u' &= 4x & v' &= 15x^2 \end{align}uu′​=2x2+5=4x​vv′​=5x3−4=15x2​​
(13)

finally giving

f′(x)=(x+1)[(2x2+5)(15x2)+(5x3−4)(4x)]+(2x2+5)(5x3−4)\begin{align} f'(x) &= (x+1)[(2x^2+5)(15x^2) + (5x^3-4)(4x)] \\ &+ (2x^2+5)(5x^3-4) \end{align}f′(x)​=(x+1)[(2x2+5)(15x2)+(5x3−4)(4x)]+(2x2+5)(5x3−4)​​
(14)

f(x)=1xexf(x) = \dfrac{1}{x} e^xf(x)=x1​ex

Identify:

u=1xv=exu′=−1x2v′=ex\begin{align} u &= \frac{1}{x} & v &= e^x \\ u' &= -\frac{1}{x^2} & v' &= e^x \end{align}uu′​=x1​=−x21​​vv′​=ex=ex​​
(15)

so

f′(x)=1xex+ex(−1x2)=ex(1x−1x2)\begin{align} f'(x) &= \frac{1}{x}e^x + e^x(-\frac{1}{x^2}) \\ &= e^x\left(\frac{1}{x} - \frac{1}{x^2}\right) \end{align}f′(x)​=x1​ex+ex(−x21​)=ex(x1​−x21​)​​
(16)

f(x)=(x2+3)ln⁡xf(x) = (x^2+3)\ln xf(x)=(x2+3)lnx

Identify:

u=x2+3v=ln⁡(x)u′=2xv′=1x\begin{align} u &= x^2+3 & v &= \ln(x) \\ u' &= 2x & v' &= \frac{1}{x} \end{align}uu′​=x2+3=2x​vv′​=ln(x)=x1​​​
(17)

so

f′(x)=(x2+3)⋅1x+(ln⁡x)(2x)=x2+3x+2xln⁡x\begin{align} f'(x) &= (x^2+3)\cdot\frac{1}{x} + (\ln x)(2x) \\ &= \frac{x^2+3}{x} + 2x\ln x \end{align}f′(x)​=(x2+3)⋅x1​+(lnx)(2x)=xx2+3​+2xlnx​​
(18)

Quotient Rule¶

Quotient Rule

If a function f(x)=u(x)/v(x)f(x) = u(x) / v(x)f(x)=u(x)/v(x) and v(x)≠0v(x) \ne 0v(x)=0, then:

f′=vu′−uv′v2f' = \frac{v u' - u v'}{v^2}f′=v2vu′−uv′​
(19)
Hint

One mnemonic that may or may not help remember this:

If the quotient rule you wish to know, it’s “low-d-high less high-d-low”... then draw the line and, down below, denominator squared will go.

To demonstrate this rule, consider f(x)=(x−1)/xf(x) = (x-1)/xf(x)=(x−1)/x. Previously, we would have needed to separate the numerator before differentiating:

f(x)=1−1xf′(x)=1x2\begin{align} f(x) &= 1 - \frac{1}{x} \\ f'(x) &= \frac{1}{x^2} \end{align}f(x)f′(x)​=1−x1​=x21​​​
(20)

With the qoutient rule, instead we recognize

u=x−1v=xu′=1v′=1\begin{align} u &= x - 1 & v &= x \\ u' &= 1 & v' &= 1 \end{align}uu′​=x−1=1​vv′​=x=1​​
(21)

so

f′=x⋅1−(x−1)⋅1x2=1x2f' = \frac{ x \cdot 1 - (x-1) \cdot 1}{x^2} = \frac{1}{x^2}f′=x2x⋅1−(x−1)⋅1​=x21​
(22)

This was obviously harder than the old way, but there are other cases where it is helpful to do the quotient rule! Here are some examples you can try:

f(x)=x2−1x4+2\displaystyle f(x) = \frac{x^2 -1}{x^4 + 2}f(x)=x4+2x2−1​

u=x2−1v=x4+2u′=2xv′=4x3\begin{align} u &= x^2 -1 & v &= x^4 +2 \\ u' &= 2x & v' &= 4x^3 \end{align}uu′​=x2−1=2x​vv′​=x4+2=4x3​​
(23)

so

f′(x)=(x4+2)⋅(2x)−(x2−1)⋅(4x3)(x4+2)2=−2x5+4x+4x3x8+4x4+4\begin{align} f'(x) &= \frac{ (x^4 + 2) \cdot (2x) - (x^2 - 1) \cdot (4x^3)}{(x^4 +2)^2}\\ &= \frac{-2x^5 + 4x +4x^3}{x^8 + 4x^4 + 4} \end{align}f′(x)​=(x4+2)2(x4+2)⋅(2x)−(x2−1)⋅(4x3)​=x8+4x4+4−2x5+4x+4x3​​​
(24)

f(x)=ex1+x\displaystyle f(x) = \frac{e^{x}}{1 + x}f(x)=1+xex​

u=exv=1+xu′=exv′=1\begin{align} u &= e^{x} & v &= 1 + x \\ u' &= e^{x} & v' &= 1 \end{align}uu′​=ex=ex​vv′​=1+x=1​​
(25)

so

f′(x)=(1+x)⋅ex−ex⋅1(1+x)2=xex(1+x)2\begin{align} f'(x) &= \frac{(1 + x) \cdot e^{x} - e^{x} \cdot 1}{(1 + x)^2} \\ &= \frac{x e^{x}}{(1 + x)^2} \end{align}f′(x)​=(1+x)2(1+x)⋅ex−ex⋅1​=(1+x)2xex​​​
(26)

f(x)=(x−1)(x2−2x)x4\displaystyle f(x) = \frac{(x - 1)(x^2 - 2x)}{x^4}f(x)=x4(x−1)(x2−2x)​

u=(x−1)(x2−2x)=x3−3x2+2xv=x4u′=3x2−6x+2v′=4x3\begin{align} u &= (x-1)(x^2-2x)=x^3-3x^2+2x & v &= x^4\\ u' &= 3x^2 - 6x + 2 & v' &= 4x^3 \\ \end{align}uu′​=(x−1)(x2−2x)=x3−3x2+2x=3x2−6x+2​vv′​=x4=4x3​​
(27)

so

f′(x)=x4⋅(3x2−6x+2)−(x3−3x2+2x)⋅4x3x8=−x6+6x5−6x4x8=−1x2+6x3−6x4\begin{align} f'(x) &= \frac{x^4 \cdot (3x^2-6x+2) - (x^3 -3x^2 +2x) \cdot 4x^3}{x^8} \\ &= \frac{-x^6 + 6x^5 - 6x^4}{x^8} \\ &= -\frac{1}{x^2} + \frac{6}{x^3} - \frac{6}{x^4} \end{align}f′(x)​=x8x4⋅(3x2−6x+2)−(x3−3x2+2x)⋅4x3​=x8−x6+6x5−6x4​=−x21​+x36​−x46​​​
(28)

Note, though, that in this case we could also have expanded the numerator, divided through by x8x^8x8, and differentiated term-by-term to arrive at the same answer. The faster route depends on the problem!

Chain rule¶

The chain rule is used to differentiate composite functions, when the “inside” of the function is more complicated than what we know.

Chain rule

If a function f(x)f(x)f(x) can be written as f(u(x))f(u(x))f(u(x)), then:

f′=d⁡ ⁣fd⁡ ⁣ud⁡ ⁣ud⁡ ⁣x=f′(u(x))u′(x)f' = \dd{}{f}{u} \dd{}{u}{x} = f'(u(x)) u'(x)f′=dudf​dxdu​=f′(u(x))u′(x)
(29)

To demonstrate this rule, consider f(x)=(x−1)2f(x) = (x-1)^2f(x)=(x−1)2. Previously, we would have needed to expand this function before differentiating:

f(x)=x2−2x+1f′(x)=2x−2\begin{align} f(x) &= x^2 - 2x + 1 \\ f'(x) &= 2x - 2 \end{align}f(x)f′(x)​=x2−2x+1=2x−2​​
(30)

With the chain rule, instead we recognize

u=x−1f=u2u′=1f′=2u\begin{align} u &= x - 1 & f &= u^2 \\ u' &= 1 & f' &= 2u \end{align}uu′​=x−1=1​ff′​=u2=2u​​
(31)

so

f′(x)=d⁡ ⁣fd⁡ ⁣ud⁡ ⁣ud⁡ ⁣x=2ud⁡ ⁣ud⁡ ⁣x=2(x−1)⋅1=2x−2f'(x) = \dd{}{f}{u} \dd{}{u}{x} = 2u \dd{}{u}{x} = 2(x-1) \cdot 1 = 2x - 2f′(x)=dudf​dxdu​=2udxdu​=2(x−1)⋅1=2x−2
(32)

The results match! Some additional examples:

f(x)=ex2f(x) = e^{x^2}f(x)=ex2

Make the replacement u=x2u = x^2u=x2:

u=x2f=euu′=2xf′=eu\begin{align} u &= x^2 & f &= e^u \\ u' &= 2x & f' &= e^u \end{align}uu′​=x2=2x​ff′​=eu=eu​​
(33)

so

f′(x)=d⁡ ⁣fd⁡ ⁣ud⁡ ⁣ud⁡ ⁣x=eud⁡ ⁣ud⁡ ⁣x=ex2⋅2xf'(x) = \dd{}{f}{u} \dd{}{u}{x} = e^{u} \dd{}{u}{x} = e^{x^2} \cdot 2xf′(x)=dudf​dxdu​=eudxdu​=ex2⋅2x
(34)

f(x)=ln⁡(1+2x)f(x) = \ln(1 + 2x)f(x)=ln(1+2x)

Make the replacement u=1+2xu = 1+2xu=1+2x:

u=1+2xf=ln⁡uu′=2f′=1u\begin{align} u &= 1 + 2x & f &= \ln u \\ u' &= 2 & f' &= \frac{1}{u} \end{align}uu′​=1+2x=2​ff′​=lnu=u1​​​
(35)

so

f′(x)=d⁡ ⁣fd⁡ ⁣ud⁡ ⁣ud⁡ ⁣x=1ud⁡ ⁣ud⁡ ⁣x=21+2xf'(x) = \dd{}{f}{u} \dd{}{u}{x} = \frac{1}{u} \dd{}{u}{x} = \frac{2}{1 + 2x}f′(x)=dudf​dxdu​=u1​dxdu​=1+2x2​
(36)

f(x)=21+2xf(x) = \dfrac{2}{1 + 2x}f(x)=1+2x2​

Make the replacement u=1+2xu = 1+2xu=1+2x:

u=1+2xf=2u−1u′=2f′=−2u−2\begin{align} u &= 1 + 2x & f &= 2u^{-1} \\ u' &= 2 & f' &= -2u^{-2} \end{align}uu′​=1+2x=2​ff′​=2u−1=−2u−2​​
(37)

so

f′(x)=d⁡ ⁣fd⁡ ⁣ud⁡ ⁣ud⁡ ⁣x=−2u−2⋅d⁡ ⁣ud⁡ ⁣x=−4(1+2x)2f'(x) = \dd{}{f}{u} \dd{}{u}{x} = -2u^{-2} \cdot \dd{}{u}{x} = \frac{-4}{(1 + 2x)^2}f′(x)=dudf​dxdu​=−2u−2⋅dxdu​=(1+2x)2−4​
(38)

Trigonometric functions¶

f(x)f(x)f(x)f′(x)f'(x)f′(x)f(x)f(x)f(x)f′(x)f'(x)f′(x)
sin⁡x\sin xsinxcos⁡x\cos xcosxcsc⁡x\csc xcscx−csc⁡xcot⁡x-\csc x \cot x−cscxcotx
cos⁡x\cos xcosx−sin⁡x-\sin x−sinxsec⁡(x)\sec(x)sec(x)sec⁡xtan⁡x\sec x \tan xsecxtanx
tan⁡x\tan xtanxsec⁡2x\sec^2 xsec2xcot⁡x\cot xcotx−csc⁡2x-\csc^2 x−csc2x

All of these follow from knowing only two derivatives: sin⁡x\sin xsinx and cos⁡x\cos xcosx! For example, to find the derivative of tan⁡x\tan xtanx, use the quotient rule:

f(x)=tan⁡x=sin⁡xcos⁡xf′(x)=cos⁡x⋅cos⁡x−sin⁡x⋅(−sin⁡x)cos⁡2x=sin⁡2x+cos⁡2xcos⁡2x=1cos⁡2x=sec⁡2x\begin{align} f(x) &= \tan x = \frac{\sin x}{\cos x} \\ f'(x) &= \frac{\cos x \cdot \cos x - \sin x \cdot (-\sin x)}{\cos^2 x} \\ &= \frac{\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x}{\cos^2 x}\\ &= \frac{1}{\cos^2 x} \\ &= \sec^2 x \end{align}f(x)f′(x)​=tanx=cosxsinx​=cos2xcosx⋅cosx−sinx⋅(−sinx)​=cos2xsin2x+cos2x​=cos2x1​=sec2x​​
(39)

Or, to find the derivative of csc⁡x\csc xcscx, use the chain rule:

f(x)=csc⁡x=(sin⁡x)−1f′(x)=−(sin⁡x)−2d⁡ ⁣d⁡ ⁣x(sin⁡x)=(sin⁡x)−2⋅(−cos⁡x)=−1sin⁡xcos⁡xsin⁡x=−csc⁡xcot⁡x\begin{align} f(x) &= \csc x = (\sin x)^{-1} \\ f'(x) &= -(\sin x)^{-2} \dd{}{}{x}(\sin x) \\ &= (\sin x)^{-2} \cdot (-\cos x) \\ &= \frac{-1}{\sin x} \frac{\cos x}{\sin x} \\ &= -\csc x \cot x \end{align}f(x)f′(x)​=cscx=(sinx)−1=−(sinx)−2dxd​(sinx)=(sinx)−2⋅(−cosx)=sinx−1​sinxcosx​=−cscxcotx​​
(40)

Some additional examples to practice:

f(x)=3cos⁡x+4sin⁡xf(x) = 3 \cos x +4 \sin xf(x)=3cosx+4sinx

f′=3d⁡ ⁣d⁡ ⁣x(cos⁡x)+4d⁡ ⁣d⁡ ⁣x(sin⁡x)=−3sin⁡x+4cos⁡x\begin{align} f' &= 3 \dd{}{}{x}(\cos x) + 4 \dd{}{}{x}(\sin x)\\ &= -3\sin x + 4\cos x \end{align}f′​=3dxd​(cosx)+4dxd​(sinx)=−3sinx+4cosx​​
(41)

f(x)=2sin⁡xcos⁡xf(x) = 2 \sin x \cos xf(x)=2sinxcosx

Use the product rule with:

u=sin⁡xv=cos⁡xu′=cos⁡xv′=−sin⁡x\begin{align} u &= \sin x & v &= \cos x\\ u' &= \cos x & v' &= -\sin x \end{align}uu′​=sinx=cosx​vv′​=cosx=−sinx​​
(42)

so

f′=2[sin⁡x(−sin⁡x)+cos⁡x(cos⁡x)]=2(cos⁡2x−sin⁡2x)=2cos⁡2x\begin{align} f' &= 2[\sin x(-\sin x) + \cos x(\cos x)] \\ &= 2(\cos^2 x-\sin^2 x) \\ &= 2 \cos 2x\\ \end{align}f′​=2[sinx(−sinx)+cosx(cosx)]=2(cos2x−sin2x)=2cos2x​​
(43)

f(x)=sin⁡2xf(x) = \sin 2xf(x)=sin2x

Use the chain rule with

u=2xf=sin⁡uu′=2f′=cos⁡u\begin{align} u &= 2x & f &= \sin u \\ u' &= 2 & f' = \cos u \end{align}uu′​=2x=2​ff′=cosu​=sinu​
(44)

so

f′=cos⁡u⋅2=2cos⁡2xf' = \cos{u} \cdot 2 = 2 \cos 2 xf′=cosu⋅2=2cos2x
(45)

f(x)=tan⁡(x2+2x+3)f(x) = \tan({x^2+2x+3})f(x)=tan(x2+2x+3)

Use the chain rule with

u=x2+2x+3f=tan⁡uu′=2x+2f′=sec⁡2u\begin{align} u &= x^2+2x+3 & f = \tan u\\ u' &= 2x+2 & f' = \sec^2 u\\ \end{align}uu′​=x2+2x+3=2x+2​f=tanuf′=sec2u​​
(46)

so

f′=sec⁡2u⋅u′=(2x+2)sec⁡2(x2+2x+3)\begin{align} f' &= \sec^2 u \cdot u'\\ &= (2x+2)\sec^2(x^2+2x+3)\\ \end{align}f′​=sec2u⋅u′=(2x+2)sec2(x2+2x+3)​​
(47)

f(x)=ecos⁡2xf(x) = e^{\cos^2 x}f(x)=ecos2x

Use the chain rule with

u=cos⁡2xf=euu′=d⁡ ⁣d⁡ ⁣x(cos⁡2x)f′=eu\begin{align} u &= \cos^2 x & f = e^{u}\\ u' &= \dd{}{}{x}(\cos^2 x) & f' = e^{u} \end{align}uu′​=cos2x=dxd​(cos2x)​f=euf′=eu​​
(48)

So

f′=euu′=ecos⁡2xd⁡ ⁣d⁡ ⁣x(cos⁡2x)f' = e^{u} u' = e^{\cos^2 x} \dd{}{}{x}(\cos^2 x)f′=euu′=ecos2xdxd​(cos2x)
(49)

Use the chain rule again with

u=cos⁡xf=u2u′=−sin⁡xf′=2u\begin{align} u &= \cos x & f = u^{2}\\ u' &= -\sin x & f' = 2u\\ \end{align}uu′​=cosx=−sinx​f=u2f′=2u​​
(50)

So

f′=ecos⁡2x(2uu′)=ecos⁡2x(2cos⁡x⋅−sin⁡x)=−2sin⁡xcos⁡xecos⁡2x\begin{align} f' &= e^{\cos^2 x}(2uu')\\ &= e^{\cos^2 x}(2\cos x \cdot -\sin x)\\ &= -2 \sin x \cos x e^{\cos^2 x}\\ \end{align}f′​=ecos2x(2uu′)=ecos2x(2cosx⋅−sinx)=−2sinxcosxecos2x​​
(51)

Last, let’s look at a physics application of these techniques:

Example: Harmonic oscillator¶

A harmonic oscillator is a mass m on a Hookean spring. The spring force is F=−kxF = -kxF=−kx, where k is the spring constant and x is the displacement of the mass.

If the mass is initially displaced to x(0)x(0)x(0), it will then move according to:

x(t)=x(0)cos⁡(2πtT)x(t) = x(0) \cos\left(\frac{2\pi t}{T}\right)x(t)=x(0)cos(T2πt​)
(52)

where

T=12πmkT = \frac{1}{2\pi} \sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}T=2π1​km​​
(53)

How fast is the oscillator moving at any given time? When is the oscillator moving fastest?

We want to calculate the velocity v=x′(t)v = x'(t)v=x′(t). Use the chain rule with:

u=2πtTf=x(0)cos⁡uu′=2πTf′=−x(0)sin⁡u\begin{align} u &= \frac{2\pi t}{T} & f &= x(0) \cos u \\ u' &= \frac{2\pi}{T} & f' &= -x(0) \sin u \end{align}uu′​=T2πt​=T2π​​ff′​=x(0)cosu=−x(0)sinu​​
(54)

so

v=d⁡ ⁣xd⁡ ⁣t=f′(u)⋅u′=−x(0)sin⁡u⋅u′=−2πx(0)Tsin⁡(2πtT)\begin{align} v &= \dd{}{x}{t} = f'(u) \cdot u' \\ &= -x(0) \sin u \cdot u' \\ &= -\frac{2\pi x(0)}{T} \sin\left(\frac{2\pi t}{T}\right) \end{align}v​=dtdx​=f′(u)⋅u′=−x(0)sinu⋅u′=−T2πx(0)​sin(T2πt​)​​
(55)

A function is at an extrema when its derivative is zero. If the function is velocity, this derivative is the acceleration a and is equal to zero, a=v′=0a = v' = 0a=v′=0. This means the mass is not accelerating! Using the chain rule again:

a=v′=−(2πT)2x(0)cos⁡(2πtT)=0a = v' = -\left(\frac{2\pi}{T}\right)^2 x(0) \cos\left(\frac{2\pi t}{T}\right) = 0a=v′=−(T2π​)2x(0)cos(T2πt​)=0
(56)

The roots occur at t=T/4t = T/4t=T/4 or 3T/43T/43T/4, when x=0x = 0x=0 and the spring is no longer stretched. All potential energy has been converted to kinetic energy!
